claim: Optimal search for a hidden target is index-based: look next where prior probability x detection chance / cost is highest, then update the map by Bayes after each empty look (p'=p(1-q)/(1-pq)). Weitzman's Pandora rule (reservation value sigma with E[(v-sigma)+]=c, open in decreasing sigma, stop when best found exceeds all remaining sigma) is the known-distribution optimum for finding the best of several costly options. Gap search: online-learned Weitzman indices beat a fixed cascade in simulation only (d01); correlated values break the exact rule (d12).
schema_part: O (choose what to check next) / G (cost of checks)
agent_test: On hypothesis-checking tasks with unequal check costs, compare a fixed check order against the p*a/c ordering at equal total tool-call tokens.
audit_note: Wikipedia (index p_i a_i / c_i, Blackwell/Assaf, p'=p(1-q)/(1-pq)), Kleinberg et al. Theorem 1, Belloni et al. (simulation, FrugalGPT baseline) and Chawla et al. (sub-linear hardness for correlated boxes) verified; index rule is optimal for the one-object, independent-box model.

claim: Humans in lab sequential-search tasks usually stop earlier than the reservation-value optimum, but the profit loss from under-searching is small; risk aversion explains it only partly and rival accounts (regret, sunk cost, misperceived horizon) did not beat the plain model.
agent_test: Measure whether the agent stops evidence-gathering earlier than a computed optimum on synthetic search tasks; compare to a human-like baseline.
audit_note: Kittaka et al. (103 subjects, 3.1-3.4 searches vs 4.537 optimum, payoff gaps small) and Marcu and Noussair (177 subjects, modest early stopping, profit loss small, regret/sunk cost/horizon/risk aversion do not improve on the model) verified; evidence is mostly two lab studies plus cited literature, and Kittaka's risk effect appears only in the passive design.

claim: In a repeated secretary-type game with a learnable value distribution, people learn near-optimal stopping within a few games; first-game errors go both ways (about 25% stop below the critical value, up to 75% above it).
agent_test: Give the agent repeated search tasks with a fixed hidden distribution, with and without a memory of past thresholds, at equal tokens.

claim: Progressive stopping heuristics (ratio of interviewed to remaining) reach over 95% of optimal across multi-threshold secretary variants; simple single-threshold heuristics fail there.
agent_test: Compare a one-threshold stop rule against a progressive rule for an agent choosing when to commit to a candidate answer.

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs explore poorly in context: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 in bandits mostly lock into a greedy suffix (GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure in more than 60% of replicates); only GPT-4 with an explore hint, external per-arm summaries and chain of thought worked. GPT-3 shows no directed exploration and ignores horizon. Gap search: reasoning models help but do not remove the failure; fixes that work use an external algorithm (posterior sampling) or RL training for breadth (d03-d05).
agent_test: Run a bandit and a search task at equal tokens with raw history versus externally computed per-option summaries plus an explicit explore instruction.
audit_note: Krishnamurthy et al. (>60% suffix failures, one working config of 72/48, GPT-4 with CoT+hint+summary) and Binz and Schulz (no directed exploration) verified; Harris and Slivkins and Arumugam and Griffiths abstracts support the gap-search sentence only loosely (Harris says reasoning models help exploitation, not exploration per se; the 'RL training for breadth' paper was not opened).

claim: LLM stopping decisions are poor in a finite-horizon explore-then-exploit game: models switch at the wrong step (earlier than the optimum in most conditions, over-exploring when optimum is immediate extraction). Giving the MDP formula plus an example did not fix it; asking the model to explain why the example is optimal helped in some conditions.
agent_test: Replicate the fuse-or-extract game with our agent, with and without a forced explain-the-optimum step.

claim: Adaptive stopping of repeated sampling saves tokens at nearly equal accuracy: early-stopping self-consistency cuts samples by 33.8% (MATH) to 84.2% (Coin Flip); a Pandora's-box UCB stopper matches best-of-N with 15-35% fewer generations; Bayesian precision stopping for evaluations removes 57-97% of trials. Gap search: reward-model-free versions (agreement, token confidence, trial answers) also save tokens: Adaptive-Consistency up to 7.9x samples at under 0.1% accuracy loss; DeepConf-low 43-79% tokens; DEER 19.1-80.1% shorter chains.
agent_test: Replace fixed-N voting with window-agreement stopping and the Weitzman stopper on our benchmarks; report accuracy per token.
audit_note: All figures verified (ESC 33.8-84.2%; Kalayci 15-35% fewer generations; Pilditch 57.2-97.3%; Adaptive-Consistency 7.9x/<0.1%; DeepConf-low 43-79%; DEER 19.1-80.1%); caveat: these gains are on different benchmarks/models and DeepConf-low accuracy changes by about -0.9 to +5.8 points, so 'nearly equal accuracy' is approximate.

claim: Coverage (any-of-k success) grows near log-linear with samples over four orders of magnitude (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples), but picking the right sample without a verifier is the bottleneck: voting and reward models plateau.
agent_test: Measure coverage versus selected accuracy at k = 1..64 on tasks with and without an automatic checker.

claim: Allocating test-time compute per prompt difficulty beats fixed best-of-N, with about 4x less compute for equal performance in some settings; a smaller model with extra test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions, but not reliably on hard ones. Gap search: a hidden-state probe predicts difficulty without oracle labels (up to 50% less compute, d10); Snell's own predicted-difficulty bins lose part of the gain at high budgets (d11).
agent_test: Route by estimated difficulty and give an adaptive token budget versus a uniform budget at equal total tokens.
audit_note: Snell et al. (about 4x less compute, 14x larger model on easy/intermediate and even some hard questions depending on workload, little benefit on hardest) and Damani et al. (up to 50% less compute) verified; minor: Snell says the 14x result can extend to hard questions under some workloads, and the 4x figure is 'up to' at low budgets with PRM search.

claim: Search-as-tree (Tree of Thoughts) lifted Game of 24 from 4% (CoT) to 74% with GPT-4.
agent_test: Run on Game of 24 and a non-arithmetic task at equal tokens against best-of-N; check the gain is not task-specific.

claim: Job and price search theory: reservation-wage stopping (McCall) and sample-size search (Stigler) are textbook results; wage dispersion for equal workers is real (44 MBA graduates, 144 offers, CV 7.9%; company offers correlate 0.58-0.76 across years), so search pays.
agent_test: None needed; background for stop-rule design.
audit_note: Stigler 1962 numbers verified (44 MBAs, 144 offers, SD $43, mean $540.7, CV 7.9%; engineer firm correlations .660/.761/.577) and Wikipedia confirms McCall reservation wage and Stigler sample-size search; minor: the 0.58-0.76 correlations are for engineers' offers and 'equal workers' is Stigler's assumption, and 'search pays' is his inference.

claim: Foraging (marginal value theorem): leave a patch when its current rate drops to the environment average; field tests support it only roughly (great tits about 30% better than random; dung flies 36 vs 40 min predicted).
schema_part: G (leave a line of reasoning when marginal yield falls)
agent_test: Implement a marginal-yield rule for abandoning a reasoning branch and compare with fixed-depth branches at equal tokens.

claim: Descending-price (Dutch-style) procedures coordinate costly search optimally because price is guaranteed at the time of information acquisition; Pandora's rule with correlated boxes is only approximable (constant factor against partially adaptive strategies).
agent_test: None; note that correlated hypotheses break the independence assumption of the index rule.
audit_note: Kleinberg et al. (descending price implements first-best search; guaranteed price at inspection; coordination losses 1-2 orders of magnitude) and Chawla et al. (constant-factor approximation to best partially adaptive strategy, fully adaptive inapproximable from samples) verified; minor: Chawla's hardness is for sample access to the joint distribution and the Dutch optimality is within the paper's independent-value model.

claim: Bayesian search was used operationally (Scorpion 1968 found about 740 km SW of the Azores; Air France 447 recovery), supporting probability maps plus cost-aware effort allocation; evidence is from secondary summaries.
agent_test: None; historical.

claim: Optimal stopping can control herding and model switching between large and small LLMs (threshold policy in belief space).
agent_test: Test a threshold escalation rule from cheap to expensive model against fixed routing at equal cost.

claim: Stopping or abandoning without a reward model works on single-answer math tasks using agreement or the model's own confidence, but confidence-only rules can sometimes hurt where the model is confidently wrong (DeepConf notes overconfidence on incorrect problems with GPT-OSS-120B at aggressive filtering, and DeepConf-low lost 0.9 points on Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 while matching or improving accuracy in most other settings).
agent_test: Compare agreement-based stopping against confidence-based stopping at equal tokens on tasks with and without a checkable answer.
audit_note: DeepConf, Adaptive-Consistency and DEER numbers verified, and DeepConf says aggressive filtering 'can sometimes hurt' from overconfidence on GPT-OSS-120B, but the cited cost is a small drop (-0.9 points on one Qwen3-32B set; DeepConf-low matches or improves accuracy in most settings), so 'rules fail' is too strong; CISC not opened.
claim_before_audit: Stopping or abandoning without a reward model works on single-answer math tasks using agreement or the model's own confidence, but confidence-only rules fail where the model is confidently wrong (DeepConf overconfidence on GPT-OSS-120B; DeepConf-low -0.9% on one set).

claim: An index rule built on an unreliable value estimate adds nothing: a Gittins sampling rule on a PRM-guided tree search gave 70.5-71.4% vs 71.6-71.9% for greedy or beam (no significant gain over best-of-N), and the authors trace it to poor PRM value estimates that worsen with depth.
schema_part: O (choose what to check next) with G (do not trust unverified self-scores)
agent_test: Test a marginal-value abandon rule with self-estimated branch values against fixed depth; expect gains only if branch value is calibrated.

claim: With correlated hypotheses the index rule has no exact version: fully adaptive strategies cannot be efficiently approximated within any sub-linear factor from samples, and a fixed probe order with adaptive stopping is the provable constant-factor fallback. No measurement of the practical cost for LLM hypothesis sets exists.
agent_test: Build hypothesis sets with known correlation and compare independent-index order against fixed order at equal checks.

claim: No study found that tests a Stigler or McCall style search with LLM-simulated subjects against the optimum; Horton's Homo Silicus replicates other economics results but has no sequential-search task. The gap is open.
agent_test: Run a McCall job-search task with LLM subjects and compute regret vs the reservation rule.

claim: Per-prompt difficulty can be predicted without oracle labels using hidden-state probes (up to 50% less compute at equal quality), but the probe needs hidden-state access and offline reward labels; for API-only agents, no cheap oracle-free signal has been shown beyond pilot agreement.
agent_test: Use a small pilot of samples and their agreement as the difficulty signal; measure whether it predicts the benefit of extra samples.
audit_note: Sources (Damani 2410.04707, Snell 2408.03314) support the numbers; the API-only/no-cheap-signal clause is an absence statement neither paper addresses.
